reading.rtitle: Partner Agreement -- Invent Software and Harbrook (extract)
paras: Clause 2 -- Territory. Harbrook is appointed as Invent's partner in Spain and Portugal. In this territory Harbrook is entitled to exclusivity for the first two years. If Harbrook does not reach the sales targets in Schedule A, Invent may end the exclusivity with thirty days' notice.

Clause 4 -- Commission. Harbrook is entitled to a commission of twenty per cent on every licence it sells in the territory. Invent shall pay the commission within thirty days of receiving payment from the customer.

Clause 6 -- Support. Harbrook shall provide first-level support to its customers in Spanish and Portuguese. Invent shall provide second-level support and is responsible for any problem in the product itself. Invent is not liable for problems in the customer's own ERP.

Clause 9 -- Confidentiality. Neither party shall share the other party's prices, customer lists or technical documents. A breach of this clause allows the other party to terminate the agreement immediately.

Clause 11 -- Term and termination. This agreement runs for one year and renews automatically every year. Either party may terminate it with a notice period of ninety days. During the agreement, Harbrook must not sell a competing product in the territory.
reading.source: Alumni by Better -- partner agreement extract written for this lesson, in the format software vendors use with resellers

gist.prompt: What is this document mainly doing?
choices: Explaining to customers how to install the software in Spain and Portugal.
Selling the product to Harbrook with prices and discounts.
Setting out what each company has to do, what each one has a right to, and how the partnership can end.

items: Harbrook can sell the product in France under this agreement.
Clause 2 says Harbrook is the partner 'in Spain and Portugal'. That is the whole territory.
Harbrook keeps exclusivity for two years, whatever its sales are.
Clause 2 says that if Harbrook 'does not reach the sales targets in Schedule A, Invent may end the exclusivity with thirty days' notice'.
Invent pays the commission after the customer pays, not when the deal is signed.
Clause 4 says Invent shall pay 'within thirty days of receiving payment from the customer'.
If the customer's own SAP fails, Invent has to pay for the damage.
Clause 6 says 'Invent is not liable for problems in the customer's own ERP'.
To end the agreement in the normal way, a company has to tell the other one about three months before.
Clause 11 says either party may terminate 'with a notice period of ninety days'.

items.situation: Marta asks what Harbrook gets for each licence. Answer with the contract word.
tips: You are entitled to a commission of twenty per cent on every licence.
A right in a contract: be entitled to + noun.

items.situation: Marta asks when Invent pays. Say the clause, then say it in plain English.
tips: Invent shall pay within thirty days of the customer's payment. In plain English: we have to pay you within a month.
Shall in the contract, have to when you speak.

items.situation: Marta asks if Harbrook can sell another vendor's product too. Answer.
tips: Not a competing product. Harbrook must not sell a competing product in the territory.
Must not = it is not allowed.

items.situation: Marta asks if Harbrook has to end the agreement after one year. Answer.
tips: No, it renews automatically. Either party may terminate with ninety days' notice.
May = an option, not a duty.

items.situation: A customer's SAP crashes and the customer blames Invent. Explain the clause.
tips: Under clause 6, we are responsible for our product, but we are not liable for problems in your own ERP.
Responsible for = a duty; not liable for = no legal responsibility.

items.situation: Marta says: can we show your price list to one big customer? Answer.
tips: I am afraid not. Neither party shall share the other party's prices. That would be a breach of clause 9.
Neither ... shall = nobody is allowed. Never neither ... shall not.

listenings.text: I review partner agreements for software companies, and the first thing I tell every sales director is this: do not read the contract from the first page to the last. Read it with two questions. What must we do, and what are we entitled to? Every clause answers one of those two questions. When you see the word shall, it is a duty. Invent shall pay the commission within thirty days. That is not a nice promise. It is an obligation, and if you do not do it, it is a breach. When you see is entitled to, it is a right. The partner is entitled to a commission. And when you see may, it is an option, something a party can do but does not have to do. The clause that people forget is termination. Everybody reads the commission. Nobody reads the notice period, and then one day they want to leave and discover that they have to wait ninety days.

I have signed partner agreements with eleven software vendors, and I read every one in the same order. First the territory, because a partner without a clear territory is just a reseller competing with the vendor's own sales team. Then exclusivity. I do not need exclusivity forever, but in the first two years I am going to invest in people and marketing, and I want to know that nobody else is selling the same product next door. Third, the commission, and when it is paid. Twenty per cent paid in thirty days is better than twenty-five paid in ninety. And last, liability. If the vendor's product fails, the vendor is liable. If the customer's own system fails, nobody should expect us to pay for it. When a vendor explains those four clauses to me in simple English on the first call, I usually sign. When the vendor sends the lawyer first, I usually do not.
